text:
This had changed quite a bit now, mainly due to current pricing(aug 2023) Also with a few things people need to take into account. Let me explain because I want to help people like me having a hard time decided on xtx vs xt.
Right now, the 7900xt reference can be had for $850 via direct AMD or $780-90 via Amazon, Newegg, etc.
While the 7900xtx reference can be had for $1000 via direct AMD or $970-980 via Amazon, Newegg, etc.
I have a 5800x3d and a corsair sf600. With that being said, I could likely "run" a 7900xtx off of a 600 platinum. But id really be pushing the limits of that psu. Soooo, Id need to ideally upgrade to a sf750. Pushing the cost of the xtx to $1300(gpu, psu with tax, shipping etc).
Or I could just get the xt, which can be ran by sf600 with decent(enough) headroom for my liking. So I wouldn't have to upgrade my psu, and wouldnt have to drop $1300.
So in my case, and the case for many others its no longer 100$ for 17% better performance between the two. Its likely along the lines of 4-500$ depending on psu upgrade cost.
And the big thing to note here is, Do you need the 4k performance and if so what many arent looking at is 4k at what hz? Couch gaming on a 4k tv either at 60hz or 120hz(oled). With a few setting tweaks, the xt will hit either of those hz just fine, without the $500 extra.

Thats just my hot take! Interested to hear thoughts, arguments, etc.

text:
@sounghungi  That's insane and burning money, at least when electricity is expensive where you live. What is your resolution, refreshrate and color depth? These things make the your monitor pixel management go wild. 

I have a theory, but I do not know if it works. If it does, please tell me, but do no tell it around in the forums or something. AMD should do their homework themselves. When your monitor does support display stream compression (DSC), you could try to activate it. My theory is that the strain on the pixel management will also reduce, but it is just a theory I got after seeing the strange results from different forum members. In order to let DSC activate you need to exceed the pixel rate of your display port. For 1.4 it is about 25 gbit/ s. When you play 1440p/144hz/10 bpc your data rate will be around 18gbit/s. If you increase for example your refreshrate to 240hz, it should get to 31 gbit/s, which then gets compressed in DSCx3  to around 10 gbit/s. You could also reduce DP to 1.2 as long as has a compression method, but I don't know for sure.
You can use this for calculation if yt does not delete the link:
https://linustechtips.com/topic/729232-guide-to-display-cables-adapters-v2/?section=calc&H=2560&V=1440&F=144&bpc=10&timing=cvtrb&calculations=show&formulas=show

I'm glad these cards creating competition, but my gripe is these cards are competing with the 4080, a card overpriced by $500. While these cards are $200-$300 cheaper than the 4080, that means they are still overpriced by $200-$300. It's name inflation. The last gen 6900XT/6950XT were supposed to be competing with the 3090/3090ti. While cheaper than the launch prices for the 6900XT/6950XT, these cards are really in the 6800/6800XT tier. While they are over spec'd for that tier, it's their performance that matters. I'm not sure there is really a comparison for previous AMD gens, since they are relatively new to the high end tier, but this would be like if Nvidia launched the 1080 under the Titan series. High end? Yes. Bleeding edge? No.

I might get a 7900XTX when Ryzen 7000 X3D comes out, cause, fuck, I'm not paying Nvidia prices, but feel like they might release a 7950XT/XTX that might be the 4090 competitor. text:
Good on you Steve! I sincerely wish more TechTubers would take a cue from you and do the same. If the 7900XT, which should have been a $700 7800XT, isn't worth PC gamers' or creator's, then it's not worth reviewers time either.

Normally if you see a 37% gen on gen price hike on an item like this it has dramatically, and I mean dramatically improved over what would be expected from a newer generation. This is not that. It's not a 980 from a 788, or a 1080 from a 980. Heck, this isn't a 1080 to a 2080 jump. It's awful. If it was priced like what it is, an x800XT card then the card would be right where it should be. Nothing incredible, just a solid gen on gen jump. Instead, it is an average product with an objectively stupid price.

Barring some absurd driver fix, this product should sit on shelves indefinitely. Unfortunately, with people still paying $700+ for 3080's and $800+ for 3080Ti's, it probably won't. Or maybe it will. There are only so many $500 GPU buyers, and there's a good chance that market is drying up, and with rumors of a possible new tape out to fix a possible hardware level mistake in a year or so, it would be asinine to purchase this card. Either buy an Nvidia card if you care about raytracing, or simply wait if you don't. Or buy a used card and call it a day.

I have never, in my entire life of PC gaming w/3d accelerators, seen a new gen come out that slots in perfectly above the previous generation. Like it isn't a new generation at all, but instead part of the old lineup. Heh, and it seems like it is from the same company no less. Nvidia card, AMD card, Nvidia Card, AMD card, with each price point covered. Absolutely ludicrous, and barring using the card for work purposes or someone who has a 4K OLED (in which case the 4090 is pretty much the only choice that makes sense) then purchasing these cards hurts the PC gaming market as a whole. The $1600+ for a 4090 is no big deal imo. Flagship cards have always been really, really expensive, but we somehow lost sight of getting very slightly less than flagship performance for almost half the price. Whether the 1080Ti for $719.99, or the 980Ti, or the 780Ti...all were exceptional cards, and great value when standing in the middle of the 80 class card and a Titan. Then the 2080Ti came out at $1200, then the 3080Ti which had 2 consumer cards above it, and now this utter trash from both companies?

This has happened before in the sense that mid-range cards crept out out of the general consumers level of affordability, and it ended up really screwing PC gaming for about 5 or 6 years. I literally HAD to buy both a 360 and PS3 to play the games I wanted because they stopped porting half of the 3rd party games I played to PC. Most people aren't willing to pay over $400 for a GPU, never mind $800+ (I assume the 4070Ti will come in around there). That means we have a ton of PC gamers who stuck with their 1060's, 580's, and 1660's. Now AMD and Nvidia expect them to pay the price of a console, for a GPU that performs like a console. Even though they have to spend at least $200 on a CPU, a minimum of $60 on a motherboard (if they bought a b450 or earlier chipset), $100+ on RAM, $100+ on storage and $75+ on a PSU? It doesn't make sense to the a normal person, and if a cross-platform AAA game doesn't have the potential to sell at least a million copies, then it isn't comign to PC in the future.

Paying these inflated prices, especially after coming off the mining boom screws everyone, and as far as I'm concerned, I am done watching content on these cards barring a Christmas driver miracle.

text:
All of this makes me feel better just leaning back and wait and see. It also makes it easier to accept the bad start Intel has had with the ARC. If I'm going to wait I can at least amuse myself by keeping an eye on what's happening with the driver situation for the ARC. Intel did after all start basically from zero and has a lot of ground to make up in driver development. That also means they have a lot of low hanging fruit to pick. That's an expression used when there are a lot of improvements that are simple to identify and cheap and easy to fix. It will be interesting to see how fast they can start harvesting these and what improvements that will provide.

Once the low hanging fruit is gone improvements will be a lot harder to achieve, and they will be smaller and smaller as the drivers are refined. Traditionally AMD has shown that hardware can be significantly hampered by drivers and performance significantly increased as the drivers mature. This is what has been dubbed Fine Wine by enthusiasts. Nvidia on the other hand has usually had release drivers that were a lot more mature with mostly bug fixes for different games in driver updates and not much in the way of significant over the board performance improvements. The raw state of the drivers really suggest that there are a lot of performance left to unlock in the ARC hardware. Question is if Intel is going to be able to get it done and how much of a difference it will make.

And even if this generation was and remains a turd no matter how much it's polished there's always next gen to keep an eye on. By then the software stack should be a lot more polished from start and it will hopefully be more competitive. And I do mean competitive. I simply don't care any more about the halo products. There is no way I'm paying that much money just to play games.

text:
@longjohn526  I mostly agree, but the 900 dollar price tag (and that's the minimum price) is giving AMD bad press. It would look so much better at 800. The optics of this kind of thing could have a significant impact on sales of Navi 32 based GPUs, and those are the GPUs which AMD stands to make the most money off of on the whole. 

I really am curious about what AMD is going to charge for those Navi 32 based cards. They're going to be a LOT more expensive than the 6700 XT is right now, that much we can be sure of. However, at least one of the versions of Navi 32 is likely to end up offering the best value per dollar for this generation. Nvidia never wants to offer the best value per dollar, because that means they've failed with their marketing. They always want to be charging higher margins than their competition, and they justify it by offering gimmicks which customers will then use to justify the higher cost. I say this as an RTX 3080 owner (bought mine used for a good price). Ray tracing is massively overrated. It's either barely noticeable or not noticeable at all, OR it has such a huge impact on performance that it's not worth it EXCEPT when you have tonnes of performance to spare. I'm honestly sick of messing around with graphics settings and trying to find the optimal balance between upscaling, ray tracing settings, and fps in certain games. As games become increasingly more demanding, ray tracing performance becomes rapidly less and less relevant, as it's always the first thing you're going to want to turn off in order to get better fps. Hardware ray tracing is, even on Nvidia cards, simply not efficient enough for the visual quality it gives you to be considered an important feature. With a 6000 series AMD card, you just don't use ray tracing and enjoy excellent fps and visual quality.

text:
I still don't get the "RT" craze! In most games so far, you can't actually notice the difference, if you did a blind test, it would be 50%-50% of people guessing which is rasterized and which is RT. The games where it is noticeable like Watch Dogs Legion every car looks like a mirror or at least it used to, maybe it has been patched since then, but at launch the cars literally looked like mirrors! Completely unrealistic and terrible looking! 

The best RT implementation so far has been Spider Man remastered, but that is literally ONE game in 4 years' time with actually noticeable and really good RT! Even so you'd still get quite a bit of a performance hit at 4k to the point where you might need to enable DLSS or FSR which means it actually lowers visual fidelity when you are enabling RT to increase visual fidelity! It the same as enabling ultra-quality textures but lowering the resolution in order to play at 60fps, it doesn't make any sense! I get that DLSS and FSR are slightly better at reconstructing a bit higher quality picture over just reducing resolution, but they also introduce a lot more blurring, ghosting, shimmering, interlacing, etc... 

So, to me RT is not a selling point yet and won't be for at least another 2 years! DLSS and FSR have never been a selling point, they are garbage at 1080p, so no point in using them with lower end cards, while they don't make any sense for 4k when you want the best visual quality! 

The only selling point Nvidia has had over AMD that is REAL and tangible and useful has been their media engine. For streaming and coding and encoding in the popular applications they've been much better, though it needs revisiting now with the 7000 series with AMD introducing a new media engine and supporting AV. Even streaming is a limited thing, the large majority of gamers don't stream and never have! Its not something that a lot of people do, even at Twitch there are maybe 5000 people streaming at each given hour, so maybe 100k people streaming monthly, but there are literally tens and tens of millions of PC gamers, streaming is like 0.1% of the market!

text: @RNG 999  That's factually wrong. RDNA3 is MUCH cheaper to produce than ADA. The estimated bill of material for both have already been released. ADA is on a huge monolithic die on TSMC 4nm (it's most expensive consumer node). RDNA3 is a chiplet based die on cheaper 5nm and 6nm. Both 5nm and 6nm nodes are much cheaper, have much higher yields, and the smaller chiplets make those yields drastically higher. That's why AMD moved to chiplet designs. They have a much lower production cost. I'd be extremely surprised if Nvidia and Intel didn't move to chiplet designs in the next couple generations, because it drastically cuts cost at almost zero performance loss. I hate Nvidia as a company, but AMDs profit margins this gen are much higher than Nvidia's. The 7900xt is overpriced because they didn't want to cut into sales of the 6000 series,  as that would mean they'd have to lower the prices on the older cards. It's the same reason the 4080 is overpriced.

For hardcore optimistic holders it meas their money are blocked until recession is over and they risks a lot if stock never return back.

There are many reason why AMD's stocks will NOT return back:
   - CPU market as overall  is today dominated by RISC (mostly ARM, ESP32, RISC-V etc.) and x86 decreases and decreases
   - server market is now under heavy ARM pressure (10% gain every year is rocket fast grow)
   - even the biggest stronghold of x86 is under ARM siege (look how powerful is 8-core RK3588, consumes single digit Watts and cost a fraction of PC)
   - laptops are demolished by Apple's ARM while Qualcomm and Mediatek are starting delivering cheap Win10 ARMbooks.
   - technical reasons as using outdated x86 CISC instruction set but internally functioning as RISC CPU (which causes unnecessary CISC-to-RISC translation burning energy and transistors.... and money and workhours). Another thing is variable instruction length of x86 (each instruction can have 1 byte up to 15 bytes which makes huge problem for parallel decoding, AMD uses sophisticated predictors for 4 decode width, while Apple can decode 8 instructions because ARM has RISC's fixed-length 4 byte encoding).
   - technical superiority of ARM is multiplied by SVE extensions for vector - flexible 128-bit up to 2048-bit long vectors supported (scalable width).
   - there are extensions also for matrix computing SME and SME2 which is light-years ahead x86's AVX512.
   - the last thing is that ARM can drop 32-bit support (and they already did it with Cortex X2 and X3, also Apple did that in 2017) because AArch32 and AArch64 are two different not compatible ISAs (with different binary encodings, registers, PC behavior, two decoders needed which the old one can be dropped)  while x86 cannot drop 32-bit mode because 64-bit mode is an extension of the older one (it saves some transistors though).

For GPU side it looks also bad:
   - license GPU Immortalis from ARM has Ray-tracing support now!!!
   - Qualcomm's GPU Adreno has Ray-tracing support for 2023 too!!!
   - Apple will join that Ray-tracing train soon
   - Apple proved that mobile GPU can be scaled into gigantic GPU which can beat desktop cards (while keeps high efficiency from mobile)
   - all this is huge threat (especially when AMD's GPU in Exynos 2200 showed that AMD cannot replicate same efficiency even they tried hard. I guess it's the same issue as Samsung hired best AMD's CPU engineers from Bobcat/Jaguar team and those developed Samsung's own Monsoose CPU lineup which failed in compare to Apple and even ARM's license Cortex cores).


I'm very skeptical about AMD future. X86 CPU lineup is inevitably dying and AMD has no backup plan (ARM based CPU to mitigate x86 cons). AMD developed ARM CPU under Jim Keller called K12 back in 2015 but it was cancelled after tape out (this means development was finished and they just throw it to the garbage). Jim Keller as chief CPU architect immediately resigned because he knew all the pros and cons between x86 and ARM. He knew RISC-based ISA is the inevitable future long time before majority of other engineers realized that (including myself).

Also Apple M2 has 40% higher IPC than new AMD Zen 4 architecture. Even worse is that license Cortex X3 has 10% higher IPC than Zen 4 and everybody can buy license (just like NEC and AMD did manufactured 8088 CPUs licensed from Intel in 1980's). ARM license server platform allows up to 512-cores with multiple chiplets (can have max 256 cores each), DDR5, PCIe 5.0, CXL. text:
It's really easy to say "just spend the $100 more for the XTX"... But you can say that about literally every computer component... "Just get the faster RAM, it's only $50 more". "Just get the bigger SSD, it's better value". "Just get the better motherboard, it has better IO"... "Just pay the extra $100 for your monitor, it has better refresh rate"... Those $100 extra here and $50 extra there add up very fast, especially if you're building an entire system.

Everyone has their budget constraints and at the end of the day, while the XTX might be better value, the XT is still good value when you compare it to pretty much every Nvidia card, it's only bad when you compare it to the XTX. 6800 XT's are basically impossible to find now in Australia and the rest of the 6000 stock is drying up fast, so I really think this review is being overly critical of the value of the card when you're putting it in the top half of your own chart.

author: @NadeemAhmed-nv2br

text:
​ @NadeemAhmed-nv2br  That's making a lot of assumptions. Does the person have the CPU even capable of driving the XTX? Do they have a monitor that can display higher refresh rates or higher resolutions? It's pretty pointless recommending a 7900 XTX to someone playing on a 1080P 60hz monitor. In that case they'd be far better off getting the XT model and putting that $100 USD towards a better monitor, or if they already have a decent monitor maybe they're still gaming on a Ryzen 2600 and getting a 5600x would be a far better upgrade.

For me I enjoy all types of games, but especially competitive games and I only play at 1440P 144hz. The XTX is obviously much better than the XT, but at 1440P I'd be paying for frames my monitor can't even display and for single player games where I want better graphics I don't care if I am getting a lower frame rate.

For me $1629 AUD is already what I consider too much to spend on a graphics card so telling me the $1879 AUD card is better value doesn't really mean anything to me when I already don't want to spend $1629. The XTX could be 100% better and I'd still buy the cheaper card because I don't have infinite money.

I bought the XT. Why? Because I had to RMA my RX 6800 XT 2 weeks ago which is now out of stock everywhere and I originally paid $1450 AUD for it (this was right in the peak of GPU prices and again, was way more than I ever wanted to spend on a graphics card). If my RMA had been processed faster I would have just replaced it with another RX 6800 XT for $900 when it was on sale and just pocketed the difference. Instead I figured I'd spend the extra $200 for the upgrade instead right at the beginning of the life cycle of the Radeon 7000 series.

I could have waited for the 6900 XT to drop in price, but stock is drying up and I have holidays coming up and I don't want to be waiting weeks for a new card when I'll have 2 weeks off work so I can actually enjoy it. This old GTX 1080 I'm currently using just doesn't cut it for 1440P gaming any more. I'm sure I'll cry in a few weeks when the rest of the 6900 XT stock is on clearance for $900, but until then I'm going to enjoy gaming on my new card while I actually get a chance to play with it.

All this to say, everyone's situation is different. HUB does excellent reviews but this one seems overly negative. Yes, in a vacuum the XT isn't a great value but for the vast majority of people that's not how they buy computer components. Unless it's absolutely TERRIBLE value, they look at what they can afford and then buy the best they can afford. HUB's own value charts don't even suggest the value is "bad".

text:
To be honest this is nonsense - people just don't understand how much impact inflation has. In 2008 4870x2 costed $549, this is equivalent to $847. In 2011 6990 costed $699, equivalent to $944 today. In 2015 Fury X costed $649 or equivalent to $828. Same story with Vega 64 or Radeon VII. Let's not forget all these cards were meant to be used in Crossfire, so in theory to achieve flagship performance , one would have needed to fit 4x4870 (or there was as well 4890, I personally had 2x4870x2), or 2x6990 (4x6970), or 4xFury X (or 2xPro Duo). So like for like equivalent performance used to cost A LOT MORE than now! 2008 it was $1694, in 2011 it was $1888 in 2015 it was $1656, in 2022 it is ONLY $1000, or $1600 if you go with NVIDIA 4090. Same story for NVIDIA. Yes their cards were ~$400, but you needed 3 of them to get what was at the time "top performance". 

So what exactly is getting more expensive? If you say - how about $300-400 R9 290/390/480/580/590/RX5700XT? What is about it? they were mid-range cards, they were NOT high-end. 

And yes - I would like to see them for less money as well, but it is fact that high-end didn't become more expensive, we just become poorer due to inflation.

author: @DuBstep115

text:
@DuBstep115  No it is not. High-end, Enthusiast, mainstream-performance, mid-range, low-end, value etc. are market segments, they have no relation to what company offers or the language, GPU market segments are agnostic what AMD or NVIDIA offers.

Some companies only offer value products, For example Intel clearly launched value oriented GPUs... are you saying A770 is high-end? Don't be stupid!

It same like saying - most Luxurious car Volkswagen is offering right now is Passat, therefore Passat is "Luxury Limousine", in the same segment as Mercedes S-Class and BMW 7-Series. Nope... when Volkswagen offered Phaeton they had car in "Luxury Limousine" segment, when they stopped offering it, they only have medium-size saloon on offer, it does not automatically become "Luxury Limousine" by virtue of being largest and most premium car company has on offer at that time.

Same for GPUs - R9 290/390/480/580/590 and RX5700XT were mid-range/mainstream. They were not competing against 780Ti, Titan, 980Ti,1080Ti, 2080Ti etc. There were high-end models at times in between - Fury X, Vega 64, Radeon VII etc. For example Fury X was a competitor with 980Ti, both launched in 2015 and both priced at $649 and both offering similar performance (Fury was on average slower by 2-5%). R9 390X was launched same year, costed $429 and competed with GTX 970 which costed $379, but was as well 10% slower. 

5700XT was clearly a mid-range products in ~$400 price bracket competing with 2070 at similar price (it was ~$450, but as well ~5% faster on average). There was still 2080 (mainstream/performance), 2080Ti (enthusiast) and RTX Titan (high-end). Overtime, RX5700XT got better, but overtime Nvidia as well launched 2070 Super... so maybe by the end of life RX5700XT got optimised from mid-range into mainstream/performance, but definitely not high-end. 

Now sure lines between segments are often blurry - there is no defined line between low-end/value, or mid-range/performance/mainstream/upper-mid, or between Enthusiast/high-end. In fact mid-range could as well be called "value" as long as cost per frame is competitive. Sometimes "flagship" model is marketed as "enthusiast", sometimes as "high-end". But some basic common sense can be used in cases like 5700XT or Intel A770 to clearly determine there products are not high-end. 

You simply don't understand how market segmentation works... and seems like you don't have common sense either.

text:
@ThunderingRoar  First of all, not everything has to follow the inflation, but the key point here is that $1000 for "flagship" is rip-off and they used to be "way cheaper" - No they were not cheaper! Adjusted for inflation all past AMD flagships where in range of $800-950... ALL OF THEM! Check launch MSRP and year of release, then apply inflation and you will see.

As well - yes multi-GPU solutions matter. It does not matter how company achieves the "high-end" market, whenever they do single die 1000mm2 in size, or they do 4x250mm2 chiplets, or they do separate cards on different PCBs connected via PCIE. The "high-end" used to be 3-way GTX480, or Quad-CF HD3870... now it is single 7900XTX card with chiplet design vs. large monolithic die in 4090. This is not really a controversial statement.

Navi21 was chip going from 6800 (XL) to 6950XT (KXTX), so don't get confused. The correct comparison between generations is 6900XT > 7900XTX and 6800XT > 7900XT. So yes 7900XT should have been called 7800XT really and I hate this bushtit calling both cards "7900", but neither is 6800 (non-XT) is right comparison. I mean sure there are Rumours of 7950XT and XTX and 7990XTX... but anyone's guess is as good as mine. I personally think that they only going to release one more card above 7900XTX, called whatever it will be called (maybe 7950XTX or 7990XTX) and that will be generational replacement for 6950XT.

So with that out of the way 6800XT>7900XT- we have jump from ~$759 ($649 MSRP 2020) to $899. Yes that is jump of $140 and 7900XT is bad value for money and naming is shit - should definitely have been called 7800XT (not as bad as 4080 12GB, but not far from it, certainly same reason). I do not argue with that, but neither it is flagship card. The XTX however compares quite well with 6900XT - it launched at $999 ($1169 today) and 7900XTX replaced it for lower price, but with sillier name.

As for CPU - that is simply competition and demand. There is no CPU shortage, there is still GPU shortage. As well Intel is competitive and it is competing. AMD and NVIDIA do not compete - it is duopoly and it will continue until there is GPU shortage. Yes we can assume it is coming to the end, but the reality is still that there are more people willing to pay $1000 for 7900XTX than AMD can make cards. When that changes I am sure AMD will revise the price accordingly.

All in all - in summery 7900XTX is not overpriced considering historic prices. 7900XT is poor value.

text:
I still don't get the "RT" craze! In most games so far, you can't actually notice the difference, if you did a blind test, it would be 50%-50% of people guessing which is rasterized and which is RT. The games where it is noticeable like Watch Dogs Legion every car looks like a mirror or at least it used to, maybe it has been patched since then, but at launch the cars literally looked like mirrors! Completely unrealistic and terrible looking! 

The best RT implementation so far has been Spider Man remastered, but that is literally ONE game in 4 years' time with actually noticeable and really good RT! Even so you'd still get quite a bit of a performance hit at 4k to the point where you might need to enable DLSS or FSR which means it actually lowers visual fidelity when you are enabling RT to increase visual fidelity! It the same as enabling ultra-quality textures but lowering the resolution in order to play at 60fps, it doesn't make any sense! I get that DLSS and FSR are slightly better at reconstructing a bit higher quality picture over just reducing resolution, but they also introduce a lot more blurring, ghosting, shimmering, interlacing, etc... 

So, to me RT is not a selling point yet and won't be for at least another 2 years! DLSS and FSR have never been a selling point, they are garbage at 1080p, so no point in using them with lower end cards, while they don't make any sense for 4k when you want the best visual quality! 

The only selling point Nvidia has had over AMD that is REAL and tangible and useful has been their media engine. For streaming and coding and encoding in the popular applications they've been much better, though it needs revisiting now with the 7000 series with AMD introducing a new media engine and supporting AV. Even streaming is a limited thing, the large majority of gamers don't stream and never have! Its not something that a lot of people do, even at Twitch there are maybe 5000 people streaming at each given hour, so maybe 100k people streaming monthly, but there are literally tens and tens of millions of PC gamers, streaming is like 0.1% of the market!

@eranbraun2  because even if there is still some market for the old gpus, the longer you wait the less value you can re-sell them for. Of course you could just keep it "just in case" but you would probably not use it again unless you build an other machine.
By changing card you kinda spend almost the same overall, but without the always lower performance.

An example just to make it clearer:
If every gen you get +30% performance and value of previous gen drops by "200 dollars" in the used market
After 3 gen you have spent 600 dollars but for 6 years you've had always the "top spec"

If you wait 6 years the card you have now will probably be either destroyed by new cards or on par with the lowest budget ones (like 980 vs 3060)

But in doing so you also get:
- constant warranty (every 2 year at least in EU)
- no need to open the card to change thermal paste or else
- support for latest features that could be hardware related
- likely better efficiency 

Worst case scenario you end up spending 100-400 dollar more in a 6 years age. Which is about 2,5-10 dollar a month in difference.

@sammiller6631  I don't think you understood that post. Have a look at my Post #2, it lists all modern GeForce cards, and it is arranged from the most value to the least value.

The value is calculated based upon comparing the MSRP cost to the Percentage of Transistors compared to the Flagship of the same Family.

According to that list, the GTX 1650-Super has been the highest value Nvidia card. You simply get More Hardware for Less Money.

So how did I arrive to my "best upgrade path" from that list? I started with the earliest card, and the weakest card. This was the GTX 750 (it ranks second on the list). Then went to upgrade it to the next generation (GTX 900) with the same Class (eg GTX 950) or Higher. This lead to the GTX 960. And so on and so forth.

Wait to see how the main GPU manufacturers look at abysmal sales and react with price cuts and/or retailers put their inventory up for sales to get the units moving - but more importantly (seems to be more of an AMD issue atm) how driver development helps iron out bugs and drive performance gains over these early numbers with reference models. AMD's drivers for the 6000 series were fantastic there for ages but in the past number of months have been horrendous, so many black screen issues. Does seem like they're aware of the backlash and are working on it though, so hopefully in the new year most of the bugs will be ironed out. 

tldr: probably best to hold off to see how pricing and performance levels out before buying into the new gen of GPU's.

text: I’m not saying it’s good or even okay, but I disagree that it’s as bad as some people say in these comments (worse than 4800 12g?…common fan bois). Adding letters to names to differentiate performance is a well established tradition in computing—eg 5700 vs 5700xt, 3070 vs 3070Ti, 12900k vs 12900ks, etc. the issue here is that the letters chosen are too similar, and also seem unnecessary. But the fact of adding letters is not new or bad in and of itself.  And no, it’s not the same as or even comparable to the 4080 12g fiasco—the vram capacity is not traditionally part of the naming convention of GPUs, and it’s not normal to have GPUs with same name other than vram. Thus, it’s a clear attempt to confuse people. Adding the letter is not same because people know that different letters in the name mean different performance tiers.
